spans.note: Restates research question and dataset scope (146,028 dyads, 4 leagues, 2012-2013 season)

spans.assertion: the hypothesis that referees favor giving red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported
the adjusted probability of a red card is 0.10 percentage points higher for dark-skinned than light-skinned players, non-significant (95% CI -0.08 to 0.30 pp; p=0.288)
adjusted risk difference is 0.1048 percentage points (95% CI [-0.0842, 0.3012]; p=0.288)
adjusted odds ratio is 1.088 (95% CI [0.933, 1.269]; p=0.283)
the analytic sample comprises 115,603 dyads with complete data, 79.2% of the original dataset
there were 1,455 red card events, a 1.26% overall rate
a sensitivity analysis was run comparing extreme skin-tone groups (very dark 0.75-1.0 vs very light 0-0.25)
the extreme-group comparison found a statistically significant difference (adjusted OR=1.198, 95% CI [1.022,1.405], p=0.026; adjusted RD=0.23pp), suggesting potential bias at the extremes
point estimate of the risk difference is 0.1048 percentage points
95% CI for the risk difference is [-0.0842, 0.3012] percentage points
p-value for the risk difference is 0.2880

adjusting for games together, position, league, and player characteristics, dark-skinned players (≥0.5) have a 0.10pp higher red-card probability than light-skinned players (<0.5), a non-significant difference since the CI includes zero, giving insufficient evidence for the hypothesis
odds ratio is 1.0879
95% CI for the odds ratio is [0.9329, 1.2685]
p-value for the odds ratio is 0.2826
the odds of a red card are 1.09x higher for dark- vs light-skinned players but this is not statistically significant, since the CI includes the null value 1.0, consistent with no effect
the unit of analysis is the player-referee dyad (N=115,603), representing all games a given player and referee encountered each other across their careers
115,603 dyads were analyzed, 79.2% of the original 146,028
1,455 dyads had at least one red card (1.26%)
the dark skin group contains 18,178 dyads (15.7%)
the light skin group contains 97,425 dyads (84.3%)
there are 1,419 unique players
there are 2,904 unique referees
on average there are 81.5 dyads per player and 39.8 dyads per referee
skin tone was dichotomized at 0.5 into a dark group (≥0.5, n=18,178) and a light group (<0.5, n=97,425)
skin tone was rated independently by two raters on a scale from "very light" (0) to "very dark" (1) based on player profile photos
the average of the two raters' ratings was used as the skin tone measure
inter-rater correlation was r=0.923, described as high reliability
the logistic regression model adjusted for 8 confounders: games in dyad, player position (12 categories), league country (4 categories), height, weight, age, yellow cards in dyad, and goals in dyad
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone data (no profile photo or rater assessment)
9,018 dyads (7.2% of those with skin tone data) were excluded for missing covariates, split as 8,461 missing position, 46 missing height, 753 missing weight
115,603 of 146,028 dyads (79.2%) were ultimately analyzed

spans.note: "Comparison of excluded vs included dyads:" list header

spans.assertion: excluded dyads (missing covariates) had a 1.22% red card rate and 19.2% dark skin
included dyads had a 1.26% red card rate and 15.7% dark skin
the minor differences between excluded and included dyads suggest limited selection bias, though excluded dyads had a slightly higher proportion of dark-skinned players
no transformations were applied to continuous variables (games, height, weight, age, yellow cards, goals); original scale was used
internal checks using standardized versions of the variables confirmed numerical stability
the primary model was logistic regression with heteroskedasticity-robust (HC1) standard errors
risk difference was estimated via an Average Marginal Effect approach: predicted probabilities computed under dark-skin=1 and dark-skin=0 counterfactuals per dyad, then averaged across dyads
confidence intervals for the risk difference were computed via nonparametric bootstrap (500 iterations, resampling at the dyad level), using the percentile method
no sample weights were applied
robust HC1 standard errors were used for the odds ratio
bootstrap standard errors were used for the risk difference
fixed effects were not used despite the nested data structure
each dyad was treated as independent in the analysis despite nesting within players and referees
model fit (pseudo R-squared, McFadden) is 0.073, indicating about 7.3% of deviance explained
the hypothesis that referees give more red cards to dark-skinned players is not supported by the analysis
the effect magnitude is very small (0.10pp), less than 1% of the 1.25% baseline rate, equivalent to about one extra red card per 1,000 dyads
the 95% CI for the risk difference includes zero, so the true effect could be negative, zero, or positive
both the risk difference (p=0.288) and odds ratio (p=0.283) fail to reach significance at α=0.05, so the null of no difference cannot be rejected
both the primary (risk difference) and secondary (odds ratio) estimands show non-significant results with CIs spanning the null
results vary by skin tone cutpoint: the primary ≥0.5/<0.5 split is non-significant (p=0.288) while the extreme ≥0.75/≤0.25 split is significant (p=0.026, OR=1.20, RD=0.23pp)
this pattern suggests any bias may be concentrated at the extremes of skin tone, but the hypothesis as tested with the midpoint split is not supported
unadjusted risk differences vary substantially by league: England +0.21pp, Germany +0.57pp (dark higher), France -0.58pp, Spain -0.51pp (light higher)
this cross-league inconsistency undermines a general conclusion of systematic referee bias
dichotomizing skin tone into binary categories loses information and may obscure dose-response relationships; sensitivity results suggest non-linear, extreme-concentrated effects
because dyads are nested within players (avg 81/player) and referees (avg 40/referee), standard errors may be underestimated even though robust SEs partially address this
clustered standard errors or multilevel models would have been preferable but were not implemented
skin tone is measured at the player level while the outcome is measured at the dyad level, complicating causal interpretation

despite covariate adjustment, certain confounders were not fully captured or available: playing style/aggression, player reputation/disciplinary history, full referee characteristics, and match-level factors
missing-data exclusions (14.7% missing skin tone, 7.2% additionally missing covariates) plus excluded dyads' higher dark-skin proportion (19.2% vs 15.7%) could bias results toward the null

skin tone measurement error is possible since it relies on static profile photos rather than in-game appearance, uses subjective (though highly reliable) ratings, and dichotomization amplifies misclassification
dark-skinned players may play different (e.g., more defensive) positions increasing red card risk; the model adjusted for position/yellow cards/goals but residual confounding remains possible
skin tone distribution may vary by player quality or league tier, potentially confounding the relationship
since the dataset spans entire careers but red cards are only from 2012-2013, player/referee characteristics may have changed over time, introducing temporal confounding
referee country-level bias measures (from online samples) may not reflect individual referee biases (ecological fallacy)
if similar null findings from other observational studies go unreported, the overall evidence base may be distorted by publication/reporting bias
the analysis assumes conditional exchangeability — that adjusting for measured covariates makes dark- and light-skinned players comparable in red card risk — an unverifiable assumption
the analysis assumes positivity (both groups represented across covariate strata), generally satisfied given the large sample
the analysis assumes correct model specification (logistic regression with linear covariate effects), though sensitivity analyses suggest some non-linearity
the analysis assumes no measurement error in skin tone ratings and covariates, likely violated for the subjective skin tone ratings
the analysis treats dyads as independent, an assumption violated by clustering within players and referees; robust SEs only partially address this
all continuous predictors have VIF < 3 (games 1.81, height 2.70, weight 2.73, age 1.05, yellowCards 1.52, goals 1.24), indicating acceptable collinearity
the model converged successfully in all primary and sensitivity analyses
pseudo R-squared is 0.073, indicating modest explanatory power
unadjusted red card rates are 1.24% for light skin and 1.32% for dark skin, an unadjusted risk difference of 0.08pp
unadjusted red card rates by position are: defenders 1.64% (highest), goalkeepers 1.27%, forwards 1.03%, midfielders 1.04% (lowest)
the extreme-group sensitivity sample comprised 99,645 dyads (83,655 very light; 15,990 very dark)
the extreme-group adjusted OR is 1.198 (95% CI [1.022,1.405]; p=0.026)
the extreme-group adjusted risk difference is 0.229 percentage points
the significant extreme-group result suggests potential bias at the extremes, though the effect remains small (~19% relative increase from a 1.21% baseline)
unadjusted risk differences by league are Germany +0.57pp, England +0.21pp (favoring the hypothesis), France -0.58pp, Spain -0.51pp (opposite direction)
this cross-league variation suggests context-specific factors (league culture, referee training, player composition) may moderate any skin tone/red card relationship
the overall analysis of 115,603 dyads finds insufficient evidence that referees systematically give more red cards to dark-skinned players
the adjusted risk difference is very small (0.10pp), non-significant (p=0.288), with a CI that includes zero
the extreme-group sensitivity analysis reveals a statistically significant effect (OR=1.20, p=0.026), suggesting potential bias may exist at the extremes
inconsistent findings across skin-tone definitions, league heterogeneity, and methodological limitations together warrant cautious interpretation
the primary hypothesis, operationalized with the midpoint cutoff (≥0.5 vs <0.5), is not supported by the available evidence
future research should use continuous/categorical skin-tone measures, multilevel modeling, and match-level data collection to reduce confounding — improvements not carried out in this analysis
a random seed of 42 was set for the bootstrap procedures
the analysis used a specified software stack (Python 3.11, pandas 2.0+, statsmodels 0.14+, scipy 1.11+, numpy 1.24+) and is reproducible from the provided data and code files
